verses.text: On that night, the king couldn’t sleep. He commanded the book of records of the chronicles to be brought, and they were read to the king.
It was found written that Mordecai had told of Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king’s eunuchs, who were doorkeepers, who had tried to lay hands on the King Ahasuerus.
The king said, “What honor and dignity has been given to Mordecai for this?” Then the king’s servants who attended him said, “Nothing has been done for him.”
The king said, “Who is in the court?” Now Haman had come into the outer court of the king’s house, to speak to the king about hanging Mordecai on the gallows that he had prepared for him.
The king’s servants said to him, “Behold,  Haman stands in the court.” The king said, “Let him come in.”
So Haman came in. The king said to him, “What shall be done to the man whom the king delights to honor?” Now Haman said in his heart, “Who would the king delight to honor more than myself?”
Haman said to the king, “For the man whom the king delights to honor,
let royal clothing be brought which the king uses to wear, and the horse that the king rides on, and on the head of which a crown royal is set.

Let the clothing and the horse be delivered to the hand of one of the king’s most noble princes, that they may array the man whom the king delights to honor with them, and have him ride on horseback through the city square, and proclaim before him, ‘Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delights to honor!’”

Then the king said to Haman, “Hurry and take the clothing and the horse, as you have said, and do this for Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king’s gate. Let nothing fail of all that you have spoken.”

Then Haman took the clothing and the horse, and arrayed Mordecai, and had him ride through the city square, and proclaimed before him, “Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delights to honor!”
Mordecai came back to the king’s gate, but Haman hurried to his house, mourning and having his head covered.

Haman recounted to Zeresh his wife and all his friends everything that had happened to him. Then his wise men and Zeresh his wife said to him, “If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of Jewish descent, you will not prevail against him, but you will surely fall before him.”
While they were yet talking with him, the king’s eunuchs came, and hurried to bring Haman to the banquet that Esther had prepared.

footnotes.content: The king's sleepless night—what we'd dismiss as mere insomnia—turns out to be the hinge of history. God often works through small things that seem like nothing at the moment: a restless night, a chance conversation, a half-forgotten deed. When we can't sleep, we don't always realize He's arranging mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The chronicles remember what the king had forgotten—and what Mordecai never asked to be remembered for. He'd stopped a plot long ago, said nothing, and moved on. Grace often works in such quiet people, those who do the right thing without demanding credit. The record, though, keeps score.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king asks what honor is due, only to learn that none has been given. There's a grief in that moment—not his grief, but ours, watching an injustice laid bare. Yet the very fact that it troubles the king means the door is opening. Sometimes the Lord works by letting inequity be seen, and then moving the heart of a ruler.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Haman enters the outer court at that exact moment—eager to ask for Mordecai's death. He walks in planning murder, unaware that the king is about to honor the man he hates. This is how the Lord sometimes moves: He doesn't prevent our enemies' steps; He overtakes them with purpose already in motion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Haman stands waiting in the court, certain of his own importance and his next victory. We rarely see it at the time—how our confidence can be hollow, how quickly the Lord overturns what we think is settled. Pride loves to stand in courts and assume the king is thinking of it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king asks whom he should honor, and Haman's heart answers before his mouth does. He can only imagine the king would honor him—because he's been living in a fog of his own importance. Yet the Lord looks into the heart and sees not what we imagine, but what is true and small and grasping.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Haman begins to describe the honor—splendid things, royal garments, a noble's guidance. He's painting his own dream, his own hunger for status. And the irony cuts deep: he'll get to give these very honors to the man he despises. What we grasp for often comes to our hands, but not the way we imagined.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Royal garments, the king's own horse—the trappings of power and dignity. Haman knows exactly what these mean; he knows they're the things that matter in a palace. But the Lord shows us that these borrowed glories are fragile, and He delights to turn them toward the humble.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A procession through the city square, a herald crying out the honored one's name for all to hear. Haman is imagining what it would feel like—the eyes, the voices, the weight of public recognition. Instead, he's describing his own humiliation in advance, teaching his own downfall before it comes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king says, 'Do exactly as you have said'—but for Mordecai the Jew. With those seven words, the whole room tilts. Haman's pride crashes like a wave hitting a cliff. Mordecai, whom he meant to destroy, is honored by the king's own command. The Lord's mercy sometimes rides on the back of the very words we meant to use as weapons.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Haman himself dresses Mordecai and leads him through the streets. The cruelty of it—being forced to praise your enemy, to elevate him with your own hands. Yet even in this reversal, there's something tender: Haman becomes the instrument of his enemy's honor. The Lord sometimes uses our own strength against our own pride.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After the honor, Mordecai returns to the king's gate—his place of faithful service and quiet waiting. Haman rushes home, his head covered in mourning, already understanding what has begun. The righteous return to their post; the proud rush to hide. The Lord's way bears weight and steadiness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Haman tells his wife and friends everything. His wise men see it at once: if Mordecai is a Jew, you will fall before him. There's a spiritual insight here that the world's wisdom misses—that the Lord's hand rests on His covenant people, and no enemy can prevail against that. Haman's own court can see it; only he is blind.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even as Haman speaks his dread with his wife, the king's eunuchs come to hurry him to Esther's banquet—the very gathering where his end will be sealed. Readers today hear an echo in this: the Lord moves His pieces even while we're still talking, still grieving, still in denial. By the time we've finished our lament, He's already moved.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
